sentences.text: Archaeornithomimus was an ornithomimosaurian theropod dinosaur that lived around 96 million years ago in Inner Mongolia, China.
This medium-sized dinosaur reached a length of 3.4 meters and weighed over 71.5 kilograms.
Evidence from relatives suggests it possessed ratite-like feathers and a keratinous beak, a hard structure made of protein.
A 2001 study examined 229 foot bones and found no signs of stress fractures, indicating healthy limbs.
The name combines Ornithomimus with the Greek word for ancient because the discoverer mistakenly believed the fossils were from layers dated to about 95 million years ago.
Peter Kaisen discovered numerous theropod remains of this animal in 1923 during an expedition to Inner Mongolia.
Charles Whitney Gilmore named and described the species as Ornithomimus asiaticus in 1933.
Dale Russell later placed the species in the new genus Archaeornithomimus in 1972.
David Smith and Peter Galton selected specimen AMNH 6565, a foot, as the lectotype in 1990.
Archaeornithomimus was likely an omnivore that ate small mammals, plants, fruit, eggs, and hatchlings of other dinosaurs.
Russell assigned Archaeornithomimus to the family Ornithomimidae, though recent analyses sometimes place it outside this family but basal in Ornithomimosauria.
Russell originally assigned Archaeornithomimus to the family Ornithomimidae.
The parent group of Archaeornithomimus is Ornithomimidae.
Archaeornithomimus is classified under the class Reptilia.
Archaeornithomimus lived in large floodplain terrains with braided rivers connected to the ocean that supported extensive vegetation.
Archaeornithomimus lived from the Coniacian to the Campanian, between 89.8 and 72.2 million years ago.
It is debated whether the species Archaeornithomimus affinis belongs to the ornithomimosaur group, with some researchers concluding it is not one.
Some scientists suggest there is insufficient fossil evidence to classify Archaeornithomimus within a specific group or family.
Recent cladistic analyses either confirm its placement in Ornithomimidae or place the species outside that family as basal to Ornithomimosauria.
In 1990, Smith and Galton concluded that the remains were not from an ornithomimosaurian but from a small theropod.
A third species, A. bissektensis, was named by Nessov in 1995 from the Bissekty Formation in Uzbekistan and is a juvenile dated to the Turonian-Coniacian.
It is now hypothesized that A. bissektensis probably does not belong to this genus.
